title: Quality Attributes and Software Architecture
oneLiner: How well a system must work (fast, available, scalable, fair, explainable) decides how it should be built, and ML adds qualities of its own.

what.html:
Quality attributes are the "how well" of a system: how fast, how available, how scalable, how secure, how easy to change. For ML they also include accuracy, robustness, fairness, explainability and coping with drift. Architecture is the structure of components and their relationships, chosen to meet those qualities.

Everyday version"A kitchen that cooks food" is the function. "Serves 500 diners in an hour, never runs out of gas, passes hygiene inspection" are the qualities, and they decide whether you build a home kitchen or a restaurant kitchen.

why.html:
• A sale-day crash and a smooth 25-million-viewer stream differ in their quality attributes and architecture, not their features.
  • Vague wishes ("fast", "reliable") can't be designed for or tested; SMART requirements can.
  • An accurate ML model that is too slow, unfair or impossible to monitor can't ship.
  • Patterns like pipe-and-filter give proven structures instead of reinventing them.

how.title: Learn from two traffic spikes
how.html: A shopping site crashed during a big sale: carts emptied, money was taken without orders. A streaming service handled 25 million viewers at once. It had picked the right qualities (scalability, performance) and the right architecture (microservices on Kubernetes).

how.title: Name the qualities
how.html: Quality attributes are measurable properties that qualify functions: operational (availability, performance, scalability, reliability), structural (portability, maintainability, configurability, extensibility) and cross-cutting (security, usability, accessibility, legal). "The dialog appears" is a function; "within 1 second" is performance.

how.title: Make them SMART
how.html: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-sensitive: "menus load within 2 seconds for 95% of requests", "99.95% uptime a year" (about 4.4 hours of allowed downtime). If a tester can't say pass or fail, it isn't SMART.

how.title: Add the ML qualities
how.html: ML components bring accuracy, robustness (works in rain, noise, missing data), explainability, fairness, drift adaptability, drift monitoring and reproducibility. Which ones matter depends on the problem type, the approach (deep learning, RAG…), how training is done, and the data available.

how.title: A fraud model's quality list
how.html: For card fraud: accuracy, millisecond latency, huge scale at low cost, quick adaptation to new tactics, explanations for analysts, the privacy-vs-cost trade-off, and reliable data feeds. First decide what matters; architecture then decides how.

how.title: See the system architecture
how.html: Architecture is structures, elements, their visible properties and relationships. System architecture adds hardware, ML, infrastructure and communication. A RAG chatbot has software parts (gateway, auth), hardware (GPUs), data (vector DB), ML (embedder, LLM, re-ranker) and deployment (Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD).

how.title: Think like an architect
how.html: Look beyond the model, set system qualities early, separate ML from non-ML duties, plan for model failures, allow experiments inside a stable structure, design for change, and give the whole team a shared map. Reuse architectural patterns: proven {context, problem, solution} recipes such as MVC.

how.title: Pipe-and-filter
how.html: Chain independent filters (each does one job) with pipes (data passed along): load → clean → scale → train → report. You can swap or remove a filter without touching the others. It's the shape of most ML pipelines.

demo.html: Run the sale. With the monolith, capacity grows in slow steps and failures pile up at the peak. Switch to microservices + autoscaling and capacity follows demand. Raise the peak and the reaction time to find where each design breaks.

example.html:
Food-delivery app requirements. Performance: order placed within 3 s for 95% of requests. Availability: 99.95% uptime. Usability: 90% of first-time users order unaided. Scalability: festival peaks without responses above 5 s. Interoperability: 99% successful payment and maps calls. Reliability: 99.9% of orders delivered correctly. Each of these becomes a monitoring check and drives design choices such as caching menus and scaling the order service separately.

Supplementary Adding an ETA prediction model adds ML qualities: ETA error under 5 minutes for 80% of orders, robust during rain, retrained weekly, and explainable to support staff.

misunderstandings: They decide the architecture; missing them causes outages.
'The app should be fast' is a requirement.
Only a SMART statement can be designed for and tested.
For ML, accuracy is the only quality that matters.
Robustness, fairness, explainability, drift handling and reproducibility matter too.
Aim for 100% availability and zero latency.
Targets must be attainable; each extra nine costs money.
It is a design idea with trade-offs that you adapt to your context.
takeaways: Quality attributes (non-functional requirements) qualify functions and drive architecture.
Group them as operational, structural and cross-cutting; write them SMART so they can be tested.
ML adds accuracy, robustness, explainability, fairness, drift adaptability, drift monitoring and reproducibility.
Architecture = elements, visible properties and relationships; system architecture adds hardware, ML, infra and communication.
Think like an architect and reuse patterns; pipe-and-filter structures most ML pipelines.
thirty: Quality attributes, or non-functional requirements, describe how well a system performs its functions: availability, performance, scalability, reliability, maintainability, security, usability and more. They must be SMART so they can be designed for and tested, for example menus in 2 seconds for 95% of requests. ML adds its own qualities: accuracy, robustness to noisy input, explainability, fairness, adapting to and monitoring drift, and reproducibility. Quality requirements drive architecture: a sale site that ignored scalability crashed, while a streaming platform designed for it served 25 million viewers on microservices and Kubernetes. Architects think beyond the model, plan for failure and change, and reuse patterns such as pipe-and-filter, where independent filters connected by pipes clean, scale, train and report.
